title: Coverage of the government's devolution announcement

content.content: There has been widespread national, regional, trade and broadcast coverage of the government’s announcement on devolving a share of income tax revenue for mayors across England.

BBC News Online, Financial Times, The I Paper andThe Guardian all run pieces noting that mayors of city regions will be given a share of income tax revenue for the first time and gain greater control of services such as housing, transport and skills.

The Mirror and Daily Express, and The Sun lead their coverage with Secretary of State, Angela Rayner’s line on the “devolution revolution”. These pieces focus on the opportunities focused by greater fiscal autonomy and the positive impact this will have on local services.

There is also coverage across regional outlets including the Northern Echo, Manchester Evening News, Birmingham Live, Express and Star, Liverpool Echo, Yorkshire Post, Cambridge News, BBC News London and Bristol 24/7 and trade outlets such as The MJ, Local Government Lawyer,Inside Housing and Local Government Chronicle.

The First Secretary of State Louise Haigh led on the morning round focussing on the announcement, taking part in interviews with GB News, LBC, Times Radio, BBC Breakfast, the Today Programme, and ITV’s Good Morning Britain.

There has been further coverage on broadcast including on BBC News, ITV News, GB News, Sky News, Times Radio, LBC News among others alongside regional outlets such as Free Radio Birmingham, BBC Merseyside, and Greatest Hits Bristol.
Channel 5’s Jeremy Vine featured a panel discussing the announcement and it has also received extensive radio coverage including BBC Radio 4 Today and regional outlets across all regions of the UK.

Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner said: “This is the first step in our plan to rewire this country and build a better future, where power is no longer hoarded in Westminster but is put back in the hands of local people – where it belongs.

“Our devolution revolution is about bringing an end to the begging-bowl culture of the past, and instead making sure our local leaders have the tools they need to drive the change that communities have been crying out for.
“We need every region to be firing on all cylinders if we want good growth in every postcode, and we will do everything in our power to make that a reality.”
More details of the announcement are available on gov.uk.

title: Developing future                   Chief Digital and Data Leaders

content.content: Strong digital and data leadership is essential to delivering better public services.
As technology becomes more central to how organisations operate, the need for strong digital and data leadership continues to grow.
Many experienced technical specialists want to move into leadership roles but may not have had opportunities to develop the wider skills needed.
The Chief Digital and Data Leader Programme has been created to help bridge this gap and support the transition.
Supporting the transition from expert to leader
The programme is designed for experienced technical professionals who are ready to take the next step in their leadership journey.
It focuses on helping participants develop the strategic, commercial and leadership skills needed for senior digital and data leadership roles.
The programme aims to support individuals to:
This is becoming increasingly important as digital, data and technology play a bigger role in organisational strategy and service delivery.
Building leadership capability through practical learning
The programme brings together professionals from different organisations and sectors, creating opportunities for collaboration, shared learning and peer support.

A key feature of the programme is its focus on real-world leadership challenges. Participants take part in practical learning experiences designed to help them develop the skills and behaviours required of senior digital and data leaders.
Rather than focusing solely on technical knowledge, the programme encourages learners to think strategically, build influence and develop their own leadership approach.
During the first residential session, participants worked through simulation-based scenarios centred on strategic storytelling, influence and leadership development.
These exercises gave learners the opportunity to practise responding to complex organisational challenges and explore what effective leadership looks like in a digital and data environment.
Looking ahead
The programme also aims to support longer-term workforce development across the digital and data profession.
Learning from the pilot programme will help inform the development of a proposed future apprenticeship standard for senior digital and data leaders.
The learning will help us understand what future development routes could support experienced technical professionals moving into strategic leadership roles.

While there are existing apprenticeship standards covering leadership and technology professions, there is currently no dedicated route focused specifically on preparing senior technologists for executive digital and data leadership roles.

A future apprenticeship standard could help employers across England develop leadership capability at scale and create more opportunities for talented technical professionals to progress into senior leadership positions.
Helping shape the future of digital leadership
Employers will play a key role in shaping this future development.

Organisations from the public, private, and SME sectors are invited to join a Trailblazer Group that will help define the knowledge, skills and behaviours needed for future senior digital and data leaders.

The group will bring together employers from different sectors to help ensure any future apprenticeship standard reflects the needs of modern organisations and the challenges faced by today's digital leaders.
By contributing to this work, organisations can help shape a future leadership pathway that supports both individual career development and long-term organisational capability.
Find out more
As organisations continue to increase their reliance on digital and data capabilities, investment in leadership development will be critical to future success.

The Chief Digital and Data Leader Programme is helping to build a pipeline of leaders who can combine technical expertise with strategic leadership, creating stronger organisations and better outcomes for the people they serve.
To learn more about the programme or to express an interest in joining the Trailblazer Group, contact Digitalscstalent@dsit.gov.uk.

description: How the Chief Digital and Data Leader Programme is helping experienced technologists move into senior leadership roles.

title: Misleading claims on council tax

content.content: There have been misleading claims reported in The Telegraph today saying that the government is planning an ‘£18bn tax raid’ through a council tax increase in England over the next few years.
This is incorrect. It is for individual councils to decide the level of council tax for their respective areas, and councils have not set the tax rates beyond this year.
We expect councils to take into consideration a range of factors, including the impact on taxpayers - but are clear that when they do set rates, they should put taxpayers first.
Referendum principles are set each year which are subject to consultation and the approval of the House of Commons.

Separately, we are also providing support for vulnerable taxpayers, with more time for them to settle outstanding bills and reforms to make the system fairer. From next year, households will be given 63 days instead of the current level of just two weeks to settle their bills and councils will be required to work with them on a sustainable repayment plan.

And billing for council tax will be shifted to 12-month payments by default, rather than the current 10 months, and the costs which councils can charge when seeking a liability order – which councils may seek, when necessary, to recover overdue bills – will be capped at £100.
An MHCLG spokesperson said: “Councils have not yet set tax rates beyond this year, and it’s inaccurate to suggest so.
“Individual councils decide the level of council tax in their areas, taking into consideration a range of local factors, but we expect them to fully take into account the impact on taxpayers.”

title: An update and reminder of CSHT single-focus agreements

content.content: More than 300 expressions of interest (EOIs) have been submitted since applications opened on 21 July for the new single-focus Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier (CSHT) agreements.
We are making up to 1,200 single-focus agreements available initially.
This strong early interest suggests that farmers and land managers value the opportunity to deliver targeted environmental outcomes through single-focus agreements.
In this post, we provide a reminder of the offer, designed to widen participation in the scheme, and how to express an interest.
A summary
A single-focus agreement is a simplified agreement focused on delivering a single environmental priority.
Through the streamlined EOI process, we want to make it easier for farmers and land managers to access CSHT funding without applying for a more complex, multi-action agreement.
The EOI process is available for single-focus agreements for the following areas:
You must express your interest through the online form on GOV.UK, but before you do:
After this, you can go ahead and complete the online EOI form on GOV.UK.
Depending on your land and its features, you might be interested in more than one single-focus agreement. If this is the case, you must complete a separate EOI form for each.
You will be contacted within 10 weeks of submitting your EOI with the next steps.
Please note that submitting an EOI does not automatically lead to an agreement.
EOIs for species-rich grassland
A Natural England representative will contact you to confirm whether a site visit is required and discuss your proposed application.
When contact is made, it will help you to have information prepared and available about:
EOIs for scheduled monument management
Historic England will contact you to discuss your proposed application, including if they need to visit the site.
Looking ahead
While this post focuses on single-focus agreements, the EOI process can also be used for agroforestry and woodland improvement agreements. Further details are available in the scheme guidance.
We will continue to expand access to CSHT throughout the year and share updates as new opportunities become available.
By subscribing to the Farming Blog, you'll be among the first to hear about these updates, as well as other support available to farmers and land managers in England.

title: Capital Grants 2026: 50% of budget allocated

content.content: Farmers, land managers and foresters across England continue to take advantage of the opportunities available through Capital Grants 2026.
This year, £225 million is available to support practical environmental improvements on farms and across the countryside.
The budget is 50% larger than in 2025, reflecting growing demand for investment in nature, water quality, biodiversity and sustainable land management.

Since the window to apply opened, there has been strong interest from across the sector, with projects coming forward that will deliver benefits for both the environment and the long-term resilience of farming.
To keep applicants informed, we committed to publishing updates as funding is allocated, with milestones at 25%, 50% and 75% of the available budget.
We can now confirm that 50% of the 2026 Capital Grants budget has been allocated.
Reaching this milestone highlights the continued demand for the scheme and the commitment of farmers, land managers and foresters to delivering environmental improvements across England.
If you plan to apply, we encourage you to submit your application as soon as possible. With a significant proportion of the available budget now allocated, funding is becoming more limited.
If you’re interested in learning more and applying:
We will blog again when we hit the 75% milestone.

title: Helping people enjoy food safely this summer

content.content: Cymraeg

The FSA's mission is "food you can trust". A key part of that mission is understanding how people think about food and food safety and using that insight to provide practical advice that helps consumers make informed choices.Our latest Consumer Insights Tracker, covering April 2025 to March 2026, provides valuable evidence about consumer attitudes and behaviours around food. The findings show that while confidence in food remains high, some food safety practices continue to pose risks. For example, when prompted, some respondents reported eating food past its use-by date, keeping leftovers for longer than recommended, or reheating leftovers multiple times. These findings are particularly important as we move through the summer months. Warmer weather, outdoor eating and barbecues can create additional opportunities for harmful bacteria to spread if food is not handled, cooked or stored safely. Foodborne illnesses such as Salmonella and Campylobacter remain a significant cause of illness each year, and simple food hygiene measures can help reduce the risk. That is why we recently launched our 'Stop. Think. Serve.' campaign, which encourages consumers to take a moment to consider food safety when preparing, cooking and serving food. The campaign focuses on practical steps people can take at home, whether they are cooking for family, hosting friends, packing a picnic or firing up the barbecue. Simple actions can make a real difference: cooking food thoroughly, avoiding cross-contamination, following use-by dates and keeping food chilled where needed. These habits help ensure that food can be enjoyed safely throughout the summer. Our message is straightforward: stop for a moment when preparing food, think about whether food is safe, and then serve with confidence. You can find advice and information on food hygiene at home on the FSA's pages on GOV.UK. The Consumer Insights Tracker helps us understand where extra guidance will be useful for people, while campaigns such as 'Stop. Think. Serve.’ enable us to turn that evidence into practical, accessible advice. By continuing to listen to consumers and respond to emerging risks, we can help people enjoy food safely and with confidence.
Katie PettiferChief Executive of FSA

title: Concrete Canvas: turning an idea into a global business

content.content: Kelsey Jones, Senior Engagement Advisor in our Enforcement team recently spent time with Wales-based business, Concrete Canvas, hearing how the business values the protection that intellectual property has provided them in the face of attempts to infringe on their products. Kelsey tells their story.

Concrete Canvas began with an ambitious challenge: to create inflatable concrete shelters for disaster relief. In trying to solve it, co-founders Will Crawford and Peter Brewin developed something with far wider potential – a new material that could change how concrete infrastructure is built, repaired and protected.

Today, Concrete Canvas is a successful Welsh business selling to more than 100 countries and employing around 80 to 90 people. Its story shows why intellectual property (IP) is not something to consider later. For some businesses, it becomes part of the foundation they build everything else on.
From university concept to global infrastructure solution
The material developed by Concrete Canvas is, in simple terms, concrete on a roll.
You can view Concrete Canvas patent GB2634752 here:GB2634752 – Search for intellectual property – GOV.UK

It is a flexible fabric filled with dry concrete powder, with a waterproof membrane on one side. It can be unrolled over structures such as canals or ditches, sprayed with water, and within 24 hours it sets into a fibre-reinforced concrete layer.

That innovation has practical impact. Concrete Canvas explains that water scarcity is a major global issue, and that water transported through concrete canals can be lost through cracked lining. Its material can be used to line new and existing infrastructure, including canals and reservoirs, to provide a durable waterproof barrier.
This is not innovation for innovation’s sake. It is a practical product designed to solve practical problems, and because the idea was genuinely new, protecting it mattered from the start.
Building in IP from the beginning

Concrete Canvas was aware of the importance of IP, as they say, “right from the get go”. The founders were supported by their university, which helped them access funding, advice and IP lawyers to file their first patent. That early decision proved important.
Will describes patent protection as essential, both in preventing copycat ideas and giving the business tools to enforce its rights when counterfeiters enter the market.

For many start-ups and SMEs, IP can feel abstract. A patent, trade mark or design right might seem like extra paperwork when you are focused on developing a product, gaining customers and keeping the business moving.
But Concrete Canvas shows why those protections become critical when success attracts attention.
Counterfeits threaten more than sales
For Concrete Canvas, infringement is not just about someone copying an idea. It is about the potential impact on customers, reputation and an entire category of material.
The business describes increasing issues with “bad actors” engaging in patent infringement, stealing trade marks, passing off and using its case studies and literature.
That matters because poor-quality imitations can damage a reputation built over 20 years and undermine confidence in the technology itself.
Fighting back strategically

Taking action against infringement can be difficult, especially for smaller companies. Concrete Canvas is clear that enforcement can be costly, time-consuming and complex, which is why its approach is strategic.

That strategy can include takedowns, warning letters, mediation, settlements and, where necessary, court action. The company notes that serious patent cases can last many years and cost significant sums, depending on the jurisdiction.

The business also works with a strategic IP information company to identify potential breaches of its patents and trade marks. Acting quickly helps reduce confusion among customers and others in the marketplace.
This is IP in action – not a certificate in a drawer, but part of daily business operations.
Hear from the Concrete Canvas team about their IP journey: VIDEO https://youtu.be/erVKB9p57sg
Making IP everyone’s business
One of the strongest messages from the Concrete Canvas story is that IP management is not owned by one person or one department.

The company says embedding IP management and takedown operations into its business involves the whole organisation. Intelligence gathering may involve sales partners, business development managers and customers helping identify potential infringers across global markets.

That whole-business approach gives Concrete Canvas a stronger position when it needs to respond. For SMEs, it is a reminder that IP protection does not stop once a right is registered. It needs to be understood, monitored and managed as the business grows.
What other SMEs can learn
Concrete Canvas’ advice to start-ups and SMEs comes down to three practical points.

There is no single route that works for every business. But where a business has something genuinely innovative, protection can be vital in helping prevent others from taking its ideas, knowledge and market position.
Why an IP strategy needs to be part of the growth plan
The Concrete Canvas journey is a powerful example of what can happen when innovation is protected early and managed strategically.

Its founders did not know at university that their idea would become a global business. But by recognising the value of IP from the beginning, they gave themselves tools to protect their invention, defend their reputation and keep control as the company scaled.

For any start-up or SME developing something new, the message is clear: protect your innovation early, think strategically about where to spend time and money, monitor the market as your business grows, act quickly when infringement creates confusion, and treat IP as part of your business operations.
Where to get support
If you are building a business around a new product, process or brand, understanding IP early can help you make informed decisions before problems arise.
The IPO offers free business guidance through the IP for Business platform, as well as support for businesses dealing with infringement through the IP crime and enforcement toolkit.
For start up businesses our https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/get-intellectual-property-right-step-by-step guide is a great starting point.
Keep an eye out on our events page for helpful classes on IP, in locations across the country. Find out more here Business events - GOV.UK
Final thought

Concrete Canvas shows that with the right advice, a clear IP strategy and a flexible approach, SMEs can protect not only what they have created, but the reputation and market confidence they have worked hard to build.

title: Transformation needs deliberately designed teams:  here's how we're building them differently

content.content: How talent shapes transformation

Government spends a lot of time talking about digital transformation, whether that’s implementing new technology, thinking about operating models, or delivering services differently. We spend less time talking about who is doing the transforming. The people delivering transformation often matter more than the programme, technology or operating model. At CustomerFirst, we've focused on a simple question: how do you build exceptional transformation teams inside of government? Typically, transformation teams are either surged or assembled through whatever recruitment route or resource happens to be available. But filling vacancies isn’t the same as building an expert, high performing team. That distinction matters, and that’s why we’re trying to do things differently.
Beyond a single talent pipeline
As a time-limited transformation programme, we need specialist expertise in areas such as service design, customer experience, organisational change and digital delivery.
These skills are in high demand across both government and industry, so relying on a single route into talent would limit the range of experience and capability we could bring together.

Rather than deciding up front whether a role should be filled through a secondment, fixed-term appointment, managed move or contingent labour, we've often explored multiple routes simultaneously. This allows us to compare different types of experience, backgrounds and perspectives before deciding the best way to bring capability into the team.

Our aim isn’t just to recruit faster, but to design the team deliberately. Bringing together different skills and perspectives around a common mission, so the team has the capability and ownership needed to deliver transformation.

Our team includes people who have worked in major government departments, startups, consultancies, and some of the UK’s most innovative and recognised organisations. They arrived through different routes, but the experience they describe is strikingly consistent. It reflects deliberate choices about how we build our team.
Ruby joined CustomerFirst on secondment from Octopus, bringing extensive experience in customer experience strategy and operating model design.
Raj joined CustomerFirst as a Service Design Lead through contingent labour, bringing experience from across government as well as founding his own companies.
Jack joined CustomerFirst from HMRC through a managed move and is working as a Service Designer, helping to transform DVLA Drivers Medical through rapid, customer-centred redesign.
Assessing for impact

If people determine whether transformation succeeds, recruitment has to assess more than experience. Experience and technical expertise matter, but impact comes from how people use those skills in practice.

For CustomerFirst, that means looking for people who can build trust across disciplines, challenge constructively, share ownership, make decisions at pace and keep focused on solving whole problems for users.

Those qualities can be harder to assess than technical expertise, but they are often what turns capability into delivery. For some specialist roles, we've designed role-specific scenarios and assessments with subject matter experts, asking candidates to work through realistic transformation challenges rather than simply describe previous experience. We use those conversations to explore how candidates navigate ambiguity, challenge established approaches, bring people together around a shared goal and make progress when there is no obvious answer.

This does not replace assessment of skills; it strengthens it. The aim is to build a fuller picture of not only what somebody can do, but how they might contribute to the environment needed for transformation to succeed.
Mixed teams are powerful, but not automatically easy

Building a team through different routes creates real benefits, but it also creates challenges. People arrive with different disciplines, employment arrangements and experiences of how organisations work.

We've found that those differences only become a strength when people are united by a common mission rather than defined by their role, profession or route into the team. That means creating shared ownership of outcomes, encouraging people to contribute beyond their specialism and treating constructive challenge as a necessary part of delivery, not something to avoid.

One of the benefits has been a reduction in hierarchy. People are trusted to take ownership of outcomes, regardless of their job title or contract type. Combined with shared team objectives, this creates stronger accountability for what the team delivers together, rather than what individuals deliver alone.
What we’re learning
A few lessons are already emerging.

First, transformation teams benefit from multiple routes into talent. Bringing together people from government, industry and specialist transformation backgrounds create a richer mix of experience and perspectives.
Second, adaptability is often as important as experience. The ability to learn, collaborate and navigate uncertainty regularly proves more valuable than having seen the same problem before.

Finally, the way you design a team directly shapes how it operates. Recruitment is not just a mechanism for filling roles. It’s one of the most important tools for creating the culture, behaviours and capability needed to deliver transformation. The aim is not to move away from Civil Service Recruitment Principles. It is to use the flexibility within them more deliberately.
We're building in the open, including how we grow our team. If any of this resonates, we'd love to hear from you. Get in touch with the CustomerFirst Talent team:  customer.first.talent@dsit.gov.uk

description: How talent shapes transformation.

title: The planning marathon - making improvements in the long run

content.content: Tom Warth (Chief Operating Officer) reflects on the Planning Inspectorate’s long-term improvements as the latest performance statistics are published.

Secretary of State for Housing, Angela Rayner, recently likened the Government’s target for new homes to running a marathon in under 5 hours – a challenge without doubt, she said, but achievable nonetheless.
It is an analogy that feels familiar- we’ve been on a journey to improve, but the hard yards, teamwork and long-term strategies have us producing good times.
I wrote recently about our own ‘marathon’ efforts to improve productivity and bring certainty into the planning process.
As I concluded then, there’s plenty still do, but our quarterly statistics published this week show those tough miles over the last few years continue to make us quicker.
Current performance
Here’s what this week’s release tells us:
Planning for plans
Of course, so much of our and your work isn’t about appeals.

More than 700 of you tuned in live to our recent webinar Plan, Prepare, Progress: A practical guide to the new local plan system, and we were inundated with questions afterwards (99 to be very precise), so we know plans are on your minds.
A few tips:
Infrastructure changes
On the subject of new guidance, there’s plenty going on in the world of infrastructure.
Just last week a number of amendments to the Planning Act 2008 introduced by the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 came into force.
They affect the process of applying for, and making representations about, applications for nationally significant infrastructure projects (NSIPs).
Do have a read and of course make sure you use our pre-application service to get that vital information and feedback ahead of an application.
Keep running up that hill
So, the ‘planning as marathon’ metaphor? Well, there’s certainly a marathon amount of reading to get through with all the new guidance and plenty of reform to come.

As with all long-distance races, the best outcomes happen when there is a race plan with a realistic pace. I hope you'll see from our data that, although it isn't going to happen overnight, our plan is working and the support of customers and stakeholders makes all the difference.

title: Cyclospora: what it is, and how can you protect yourself when travelling?

content.content: Every summer, a small but steady number of UK travellers return from holidays abroad with an unwelcome souvenir: a parasitic infection that can leave them dealing with unpleasant gastrointestinal symptoms for weeks. This summer we’ve seen a sharp rise in illness caused by cyclospora.
What is cyclospora?

Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that causes an illness called cyclosporiasis. It doesn't occur naturally in the UK, but is found in a number of tropical and subtropical countries, including parts of Central and South America, South and Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Africa. For UK travellers, most cases in recent years have been linked to visits to Mexico.

The parasite spreads through food or water contaminated with infected human poo. It's most commonly associated with fresh produce, particularly soft or unpeeled fruit, salad leaves, and herbs such as coriander or basil, though contaminated water can also be a source. Cyclospora is not passed from person to person through everyday contact, so you won’t catch it from someone who is unwell.
What are the symptoms?

Symptoms typically appear around a week after eating or drinking something contaminated. They can include watery diarrhoea, stomach cramps, bloating, wind, nausea, fever, tiredness, muscle aches, and loss of appetite or weight.

For most people, the illness is unpleasant but self-limiting, resolving on its own within a few days to a few weeks. However, symptoms can sometimes persist for longer, or return after apparently clearing up. People with weakened immune systems, including those living with HIV, are at greater risk of more severe or prolonged illness. Diagnosis is confirmed through a stool sample test, and while most people recover without treatment, antibiotics can be prescribed for severe or lingering cases.
What should I do before I go?
Being prepared can help you avoid illness or cope with symptoms better:
How can I reduce my risk while travelling?
There's no vaccine against cyclospora so prevention comes down to good food and water hygiene, whether you're backpacking or staying in a 5-star all-inclusive resort. Useful precautions include:
What should I do if I fall ill while abroad?

If you do develop gastrointestinal symptoms while abroad, staying hydrated with safe fluids (bottled water and hot drinks made with freshly boiled water) and oral rehydration solutions is important, and you should seek medical advice promptly if you have a weakened immune system or your symptoms are severe. If you have symptoms when you return, you should get medical help and mention your recent travel, including everywhere you visited. This helps healthcare professionals consider the right possible causes and arrange appropriate testing.
What is UKHSA's role in this area?

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) is responsible for protecting the public from infectious diseases, including gastrointestinal infections like cyclosporiasis. This work includes monitoring disease trends, investigating outbreaks, and issuing public health advice.

UKHSA does not carry out routine, ongoing surveillance of cyclosporiasis as it does for some pathogens. Instead, laboratory-confirmed cases are reported to UKHSA through the national laboratory notification system, and the agency publishes findings and advice when it identifies a rise in cases, such as during a notable outbreak. When this happens, UKHSA may work with partner organisations, including the National Travel Health Network and Centre (NaTHNaC), ABTA, and public health authorities in affected countries, to investigate clusters and ensure travellers have access to up-to-date guidance.

This is part of UKHSA's broader responsibility for health protection: tracking a wide range of infectious diseases, spotting unusual patterns or increases, and translating that surveillance into practical, timely advice for the public and for healthcare professionals.

Cyclospora is a good reminder that even in comfortable holiday settings, food and water hygiene matters. Simple precautions, drinking safe water, choosing well-cooked food, and being cautious with unpeeled produce help to reduce your risk. If you do become unwell after travelling, don't hesitate to seek medical advice and mention your travel history.

title: Using AI to support faster local plan consultation analysis

content.content: Local plan consultations can generate large volumes of feedback from residents, developers, statutory consultees and community groups. For planning teams, reviewing, grouping and summarising these responses is essential work, but it can take significant officer time before the deeper analysis can begin.

Through the PropTech Innovation Fund, MHCLG’s Digital Planning Programme has supported a pilot exploring how artificial intelligence can help with this process, freeing up officers to focus on meaningful judgement, analysis and engagement.
The initial pilot

Greater Cambridge Shared Planning (GCSP) and University of Liverpool looked to tackle this problem developing PlanAI, an AI tool designed to help planning teams summarise consultation responses. The results were promising. In the initial trial, the time taken to analyse planning consultation responses was reduced from around 18.5 hours to approximately 16 minutes.
As we set out in our previous blog post, the team were keen to find out whether this success could be replicated and scaled elsewhere in the country.
Scaling into other geographies
Five planning authorities from across the country took part in extending the pilot work to test whether the tool could deliver similar benefits in different settings:
Across participating planning authorities, the pilot produced efficiency gains of around 90%.
What did the councils learn?

Many of the planning authorities agreed the tool helped them to summarise consultation responses. There were also useful reflections on how to get the most from the process and considerations on what they would do differently next time:
Catherine McRory, Principal Planning Officer at The Royal Borough of Greenwich, said:

The pilot proved that when it is used well, the tool can play a useful role in consultation analysis, particularly where councils are managing large volumes of consultation feedback within tight deadlines. However, the participating authorities learnt that the tool delivers the greatest value when combined with clear governance, well-structured data and professional oversight.
Watch this show and tell to hear more about the recent pilots, including presentations from the planning authorities who were involved.
You can also watch this show and tell from February 2026 to hear how the pilots first got started.
Supporting innovation and choice

This work reflects the wider approach of MHCLG’s Digital Planning Programme: testing promising digital tools with councils, gathering evidence about what works, and supporting the conditions needed for wider adoption. Alongside pilots such as this, the Digital Planning Programme is also developing a variety of AI tools for local planning authorities (LPAs). This includes Extract, an AI-powered tool that helps LPAs convert historic planning documents into usable, standardised data, and a new AI planning prototype is being tested with LPAs to support the processing of routine planning applications.

Together, these projects show how AI can be used carefully and practically in planning: not to make decisions in place of officers, but to reduce manual processing, improve access to information and help planning teams focus their expertise where it matters most.

The Digital Planning Programme is combining the development of shared national tools with funding and support for locally-led innovation. This provides both a common foundation and a diverse marketplace of solutions that LPAs can adopt to meet their own needs, working with industry partners to co-design along the way.
What happens next

The next step is to continue building the evidence base for where AI can add value in planning, and identifying where additional safeguards, guidance or support are needed. As more planning authorities adopt and test tools such as PlanAI, the programme will continue to share learning openly so that councils can make informed decisions about the technology they use.

Through the Open Digital Planning network, MHCLG provides a space where LPAs can connect with peers who have already tested new approaches in their planning services, sharing practical guidance and evidence on return on investment to reduce the barriers to trialling and adopting digital tools.

The experiences of planning authorities in this pilot shows that, when used responsibly, AI can help them process information faster, strengthen evidence-led plan-making and give officers more time to focus on the decisions and conversations that shape places.

description: AI is helping planning teams cut through the time-consuming work of consultation analysis. A pilot has been extended with 5 more planning authorities, delivering efficiency gains and freeing officers to focus on judgement and engagement. But success depends on strong governance, good data structure and proper quality assurance.

title: Paying your annual fee: what you need to know
authors: Jayne Coward, Deputy Director for Early Years Regulatory Policy and Practice

content.content: When you apply to register with Ofsted as a childcare provider, you will need to pay an application fee. You’ll then need to pay an annual registration fee once we approve your application.
In this blog, I’ll explain the main things you need to know about fees.
The fee depends on the register(s) you are on
The cost of the fee depends on what type of childcare you are applying to register as and which register(s) you want to join. We set out all the fees and costs in our registration guidance.
If you are a childcare on domestic premises or childcare on non-domestic premises provider, you may be eligible to pay a reduced fee. This depends on how often you work.
Once you’re registered with us, you can add additional premises to your application. There is an extra fee for this.
There are different ways to pay
To remain registered with Ofsted, you must pay a registration fee each year.
You will need to do this on the anniversary of your registration or when your additional premises were approved. Paying your annual fee is a requirement for registration.
You can pay your annual fee:
Direct debit helps make sure you don’t miss a payment
Setting up a direct debit is easy and will help you to make sure you won’t miss a payment. To set up a direct debit, you’ll need:
We have more information on how to pay your Ofsted annual registration fee by direct debit.
We will collect the direct debit for your annual registration fee on the anniversary of your registration date each year.
Missing your annual fee means you are no longer registered
It is essential to pay your fee on time. If you do not pay your fee, we will take steps to cancel your registration.
If we do cancel your registration, you will no longer be able to care for children. Our early years and childcare enforcement policy gives more detail about the cancellation process.
You'll get your invoice by post and email
We will send you your annual fee invoice via post and email.
We'll remind you to pay your fee
We will email you once your invoice is overdue by 7 days. After the 7 days we’ll send you more reminders by text and email.
If you still haven’t paid your invoice 30 days after it’s due, we will issue you with a notice of decision to cancel your registration.
Your invoice has more information on how to pay and how to contact us.
Paying your fees on time means you can stay registered without any complications and keep caring for babies and children. If you have questions, please reach out to us.

title: Expanding Teaching Vacancies to further education

content.content: One distinctive thing about further education (FE) is that many of its teachers don’t begin their careers in education.
An engineering lecturer may have spent years working in manufacturing. A plumbing lecturer may have built a career in the construction industry before deciding to teach.

Colleges depend on people bringing practical experience into the classroom, but this creates a different recruitment challenge from the one faced by schools. Many people who could become excellent FE teachers aren’t actively looking for teaching jobs. Some may not even have realised that teaching is an option.
Helping those people discover opportunities is one part of the recruitment challenge. That’s why we’re expanding Teaching Vacancies to further education.
Why Teaching Vacancies?

Teaching Vacancies is the Department for Education's free recruitment service. It brings teaching and education vacancies together in one place, helping employers reach candidates and jobseekers find their next role.

Since launching in 2019, Teaching Vacancies has become the government's national recruitment service for schools. More than 90% of state-funded schools now use the service and it attracts over 800,000 jobseekers every month.

We’ve expanded the service to include school support staff, integrated it with applicant tracking systems used by larger organisations, and worked with the Department for Work and Pensions to increase the visibility of vacancies.
Each step has been driven by the same principle: making it easier for employers and jobseekers to find one another.

As we've explored how Teaching Vacancies could support further education, one finding has come up repeatedly in our user research: many people with the skills and experience colleges are looking for do not see themselves as future teachers.

Some told us they had only recently begun to consider teaching following a change in their career or personal circumstances. Others were looking for reassurance that their industry experience would be valued, even without a traditional teaching background.
This reinforced our view that helping people discover FE opportunities is just as important as making those opportunities easy for colleges to advertise.
Built with colleges
We’re now testing how our established Teaching Vacancies service works for people recruiting in further education and those looking to work in the sector.
Working with colleges has challenged some of our assumptions.

Recruitment is similar across schools and further education in some ways. But the language, roles and candidate journeys can be very different. This shows why we need to test the service with real users rather than assume that what works well for schools will automatically work for colleges.
Over the past year we’ve worked closely with colleges, recruiters and jobseekers to understand how recruitment works across the sector.

That research has shaped the service, and we’re now testing it with an initial group of colleges. This will allow us to learn from live recruitment activity before making the service more widely available. We expect to make the service more widely available by January 2027.
What happens next
Teaching Vacancies cannot solve every challenge facing further education recruitment, but it can make one important part of the process simpler.
When someone decides that teaching could be the next step in their career, they should be able to find relevant opportunities quickly, easily and through a trusted government service.
If you recruit in further education and would like to find out more, contact the team at teaching.vacancies@education.gov.uk.

description: Teaching Vacancies is expanding to further education. We explain what we have learned from colleges, recruiters and jobseekers, and how we are testing the service before making it more widely available.

title: Digital identity fraud risks: why OfDIA is asking for evidence

content.content: The National Assessments Centre, which sits within the National Crime Agency (NCA), has been commissioned by the Office for Digital Identities and Attributes (OfDIA) to produce an intelligence assessment into the fraud threats targeting businesses providing digital identity products and services.

The purpose of this piece of work is to further improve our understanding of how fraud manifests in, and is enabled by, digital identity services and providers, and the impacts of this fraud for providers, users and relying parties. The resulting intelligence assessment will support ongoing NCA and OfDIA strategic decision making, support the allocation of resource against threats and target response activity.
How we're gathering evidence

As part of the intelligence collection for this assessment, OfDIA has issued a survey to key partners to gather information relating to how the digital identity services ecosystem is both targeted for fraud and unintentionally enables fraud. This intelligence collection will contribute to growing the NCA and OfDIA’s cross community view of the threats.

The survey seeks information from organisations about their roles and functions in the digital identity ecosystem and the fraud threats and common attacker tactics they see across the variety of digital identity journeys their services support. Organisations are also invited to provide insight into supply-chain and third-party risks, and mitigations for fraud detection, prevention and management.
The survey went live on 10th July 2026, and OfDIA are seeking responses by 7th August 2026.
Next steps

After the survey results are received, the NCA will use the intelligence provided to undergo threat analysis and highlight key vulnerabilities to OfDIA.  The intelligence assessment is expected to conclude in November 2026.

The vulnerabilities identified through this research will be used by OfDIA to identify priority fraud risks, evaluate and improve existing interventions such as requirements in the UK digital verification services trust framework, and inform future policy development to support organisations in preventing and responding to fraud.

title: How the Joint Unit for Waste Crime is dismantling organised crime in the UK waste industry

content.content: Waste crime isn't fly-tipping. It's a billion-pound criminal enterprise in which organised crime groups exploit the waste industry to launder money, evade tax, undercut legitimate businesses, and pollute communities and the environment, while presenting themselves as lawful operators.
These criminals evolve constantly. So do we. We build new tools, use smarter technology, and work with a growing network of partners to stop them — before, during, and after the crime.
That's the work of the Joint Unit for Waste Crime (JUWC). This is what we achieved in 2025–26.
A year in numbers
Our 14 full-time crime officers didn't just process cases. They went after criminal networks.
Each number represents a network disrupted, a community protected, a legitimate business given a fairer chance.
A family empire dismantled

For over a decade, one family ran what looked like a waste business. It wasn't. It was an unlawful landfill, scrap metal operation, and waste transfer station — a hostile, deeply entrenched site that had defied the Environment Agency for years.
We didn't try to fine our way out of it. We set out to make the criminal business model impossible to survive.

Working with police, HMRC, the Insolvency Service, local councils, and DVSA, we built a case that went far beyond waste offences. The result: 23 heavy goods vehicles seized and destroyed, the family removed from their home on site, assets recovered — including land transferred between family members to avoid accountability. A £50,000 Bounce Back Loan fraudulently obtained is being recovered. Proceeds of Crime Act proceedings continue.
A problem that persisted for more than a decade is gone. That's exactly what the JUWC was built to do.
On the road
A significant part of our work happens in real time, on roadsides across the country.

In Kent, a multi-agency day of action stopped 14 vehicles, led to one arrest, and placed multiple drivers under investigation. On the Scottish borders, our officers joined Highways England, SEPA, and Police Scotland to check waste-carrying vehicles crossing in both directions.

In Lancashire, working alongside the National Crime Agency, our officers joined the arrest of a man connected to multiple sites of large-scale illegal dumping. His vehicle was seized. A prosecution is pending.
These operations matter. They're visible. They disrupt criminal routines. And they send a clear message: the roads are not safe ground for waste criminals.
Disruption is as powerful as prosecution
A prosecution can take years. While courts grind through the process, organised crime groups keep operating and keep profiting. That's why disruption is central to everything we do.

Operation 'B' targeted an organised crime group running illegal waste sites and large-scale dumping. We deregistered their waste carrier licences, seized vehicles, and worked with police to pursue individuals for other offences. The group's ability to function collapsed. They are now formally recorded as dismantled.

Operation 'C' focused on one individual running permitted waste sites across England while engaged in fraud and money laundering. We secured an account freezing order for £600,000, suspended permits, and removed waste exemptions across multiple sites. That individual is no longer active in the waste industry.
Financial pressure, regulatory action, and genuine partnership - applied consistently -can achieve things that criminal prosecution alone cannot.
A growing threat. A growing response.

Organised crime groups are becoming harder to spot. They increasingly mimic legitimate waste businesses, making detection harder and harm greater. Demand to target the highest-risk groups has grown every year.

We've grown to meet it. This year, we expanded the JUWC from 10 to 18 full-time staff, with the full team in post from March 2026. Two officers qualified as drone pilots - giving us the ability to detect illegal sites and gather evidence from the air, reaching places that used to stay hidden.

In September, we gave evidence to the House of Lords Environment and Climate Change Committee's inquiry into serious and organised waste crime. The Committee's findings are now being considered at the highest levels of government.
What this year proves
Waste crime is serious crime. It causes serious harm. It deserves a serious response.
The environment is worth protecting. Communities bearing the burden of illegal dumping deserve better. And legitimate businesses being undercut by criminals deserve a level playing field.
That's what the JUWC is here for.
Read our end of year report:
https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/joint-unit-for-waste-crime-juwc-end-of-year-report-2025-to-2026

If you have information about illegal activity in the waste sector, report it anonymously to Crimestoppers. In England or Scotland, contact the Environment Agency or SEPA incident hotline on 0800 80 70 60 - available 24 hours a day.

title: Naming a service: how we chose a name for Share Homes for Ukraine data
authors: Denise Atkins, Content Designer, Homes for Ukraine Digital

content.content: A new start for Homes for Ukraine

The Homes for Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme was introduced in 2022 in response to Russia’s full scale illegal invasion of Ukraine. It enables Ukrainians fleeing the conflict to find safe accommodation with UK hosts.

You can read more about how our team created ‘Share Homes for Ukraine data’, our new, sustainable in-house system (or digital service) to support this humanitarian crisis, transitioning from emergency response to long-term transformation.
Moving on from the old platform

As the new system took shape, it was called by a variety of names. Some of these referenced the old platform, which we needed to move on from. At other times, it was referred to as ‘future tech’ or ‘the new thing’.
We didn’t want any of these internal nicknames to become embedded, as, from experience, they can be hard to shake off.
So, before we told users about the new system, we needed to decide on the name.
Bringing stakeholders with us
Deadlines were tight, so there wasn’t time for extensive user research around the name.

Naming can be an emotive topic, especially for the people closest to a service, so we needed to bring our stakeholders along with us. It was important that everyone understood the rationale behind the new name, particularly the people who would be guiding our users through the transition.
As the content designer on the team, I invited key stakeholders across the Homes for Ukraine digital and policy teams to a naming workshop.

I began by setting out the goals and expectations for the session. We didn’t want to go with the most popular choice. We weren’t going to vote for our favourites or make a final decision during the workshop.
Understanding good names
We established the naming architecture for the system, underneath the Homes for Ukraine service.
We looked at some good examples of existing service names:
We also looked at some confusing, "bad" names, that told us little about the product or service.
We agreed that a good name:
And the name will not:

I then took our stakeholders through the government Service Manual advice on naming a government service. The system isn’t public facing, so following the naming pattern for a government service wasn’t mandatory, although we still found the patterns a useful guide to ensure we created a name that would be accessible, trusted and understood.
After that, we got stuck into the mural board to put down all our ideas for describing the system. We used a series of prompts to inspire us:

We came up with over 50 words and phrases to describe the system. Between us, we organised these words into a quadrant. We ranked each word against two criteria. The vertical axis ranked words from ‘not task-focused’ at the bottom to ‘describes the task’ at the top. On the horizontal axis we ranked from ‘poetic’ to ‘plain English’.

That gave us a selection of words and phrases that sat in the top right corner, both describing the task and in plain English. We removed the other 3 sections and used a bigger version of the top right section to rank the best ones more ruthlessly, based on our acceptance criteria. We discussed these as a group and removed a few more that didn’t fit.
That gave us a selection of very strong contenders for the name.
Research and stress testing

Following the workshop, I discussed the shortlist in more detail with our Head of Product. We played around with a few alternatives, looking at words with similar meanings, and changing the order of the words. Others were removed as they weren’t suitable for certain potential use cases.
We agreed on the most suitable name, ‘Share Homes for Ukraine data’, plus a back-up using ‘Manage’ instead of ‘Share’.
Then I went off to conduct some final, desk-based research.
Existing service names
We didn’t want our name to clash with any other services or systems, so I explored what was already out there. I found nothing that overlapped with our name.

‘Data’ was a word that came up a lot in the workshop. It can sound like jargon, but it’s commonly used and much shorter than ‘information’. So, I checked to see if ‘data’ was used by other government services. I found a few that already had ‘data’ in the name, so we decided it was appropriate to use.
Checking user research

The user researchers on the Homes for Ukraine team did a quick review of their previous transcripts. That showed us the sort of words that came up naturally during our early discovery and user testing sessions with local authorities (LAs). This confirmed that our name used words the LAs were already familiar with. It reflected how they describe the tasks they perform on the system.
Avoiding bad names
I needed to check there weren’t going to be any embarrassing moments with the name, such as an initialism that spells something rude.

Also, while the system wasn’t going to be used by the public, it might still be talked about in front of the public. So, we wanted to check it didn’t sound silly or offensive in Ukrainian, as well as English.
Choosing and communicating the name

With all the due diligence complete, we agreed on Share Homes for Ukraine data. And because we didn’t want it abbreviated to an inaccessible acronym or an initialism, we decided on ‘Share’ as the official short, less formal version.

We told internal stakeholders the new name by email, explaining the process we went through and the rationale behind the final decision. We also explained how to capitalise the name, using sentence case for accessibility.
Our chosen name works because:
We also think Share sounds warm and humanitarian. This wasn’t among our acceptance criteria at the start, but it was a lovely bonus.
Stakeholder buy-in
The whole process was also fast, taking just a couple of weeks to prepare and run the workshop, synthesise the outputs, and decide on the name.
By taking stakeholders through the naming process with us, we ensured buy-in from key people. The final name was very well-received by all stakeholders.

With clear communication about the name, we avoided something different taking hold informally, before external communications had begun. We love the user-centred, task-focused name of our new system.

title: Beyond the trees: how to make your woodland a wildlife haven

content.content: Healthy, species‑rich woodlands are more than a backdrop to rural life – they are working ecosystems that store carbon, slow water, protect soils and support livelihoods. The UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) treats biodiversity as an integral part of sustainable forest management across all woodland types, including ancient semi‑natural, native broadleaf, farm copses and productive conifers.

Diverse forests are better able to withstand pests, diseases and extreme weather events. They also provide the flexibility to meet your goals, whether that’s quality timber, nature recovery, public access or all three.
Understanding protected and priority species
Before you start woodland operations, it’s important to build up a picture of the wildlife on your site. Check local records and seek advice from your local Woodland Officer.

A woodland management plan that maps sensitive areas will help you to schedule work to avoid disturbing protected or priority species. For example, avoiding thinning near nesting sites in spring, retaining potential bat roost trees, or buffering watercourses that support species like Atlantic salmon or freshwater pearl mussel.
The aim is simple: stay legally compliant and take practical steps to help wildlife thrive while management work continues.
Special considerations for ancient woodland
Ancient woodlands, including ancient semi‑natural woodland (ASNW), wood pasture and parkland, and plantations on ancient woodland sites (PAWS), are irreplaceable.
For ASNW, keep trees native, avoid introducing invasive, non‑native species, protect veteran trees and soils, and manage deer and invasive shrubs.

For PAWS, plan progressive restoration and retain remnant ancient features. Thin and restructure your woodland to let light in, and favour natural regeneration of native species (where trees seed within the woodland habitat itself). Restoration strengthens resilience, supports specialist wildlife and leaves a legacy you can be proud of.
Getting the mix right

The UKFS embeds biodiversity into woodland design. Following best practice, manage at least 15% of your Forest Management Unit (FMU) with biodiversity as a major objective. Consider long‑term retentions such as riparian corridors (wooded areas alongside water bodies), native woodland blocks, open habitat networks, and deadwood hotspots.
Across your whole FMU, these simple ratios spread risk, create varied habitats and promote resilience without sacrificing productivity:
Deadwood as nature’s hidden infrastructure

Up to a fifth of woodland species depend on decaying wood.1 Plan to retain standing and fallen deadwood, especially large‑diameter native pieces in clusters around high‑value areas such as veteran trees, riparian zones, wood pasture and ancient woodland.

Over time, work towards roughly one lorry‑load per hectare (around 20 m³/ha). Manage safety hazards on well‑used trails, and where pests such as bark beetles are a concern, follow guidance on inspecting and removing specific host material after storms or periods of drought.
Connectivity and fragmentation

Wildlife moves through networks, so strengthening these connections within and beyond your boundary by linking habitats makes a real difference. Broaden rides and glades, build graded edges, retain hedgerows and veteran trees, and establish riparian corridors that stitch woods to the wider landscape.

When creating new woodland, extend from existing semi‑natural habitats to reduce edge effects. By expanding an existing habitat, you can maximise the safe interior ‘core’ of your woodland to limit the amount of vulnerable outer border exposed to harsh, external conditions. Design for connectivity but keep biosecurity in mind, by cleaning machinery and footwear, and control invasive non‑native species so that new links don’t become invasion routes.
Native woodland enhancement

Native woods carry the highest biodiversity value and are central to resilient landscapes. You can improve their ecological condition by controlling deer, grey squirrels and invasive shrubs, protecting soils, encouraging natural regeneration and having a diverse tree age and structure.

When creating new woods, choose site‑adapted native species and provenances (using certified reproductive material) and consider your site’s future climate. Converting appropriate non‑native stands near ancient woodland or along watercourses can deliver quick gains for wildlife and water quality.
Monitoring and assessment
Monitoring turns good intentions into results. It’s important to review your woodland management plan on a five‑year cycle. Keep it simple and carry out repeatable checks including:
The Woodland Wildlife Toolkit offers information and practical management guidance to better understand and care for your local woodland wildlife.
What this means for your objectives
Whether your aim is for habitat recovery, quality timber, natural flood management, farm diversification or public access – the UKFS gives you a single, practical framework to work from.

description: Neil Riddle, Head of Natural Environment at the Forestry Commission, explains how small, smart choices can turn your woodland into a wildlife hotspot while still producing timber and supporting long‑term resilience.

title: Slurry storage: sort it in summer, be winter-ready

content.content: In the middle of another hot, dry summer we can see our climate is changing. When we head into winter this translates into more rain, more runoff, and more pressure on slurry storage.  Getting ahead now can help protect your land, your business and the waterways your community depends on.

Slurry managed well is a resource. Slurry mismanaged is a pollution risk - to rivers, soils, and the communities downstream. The choices made now, in summer, shape what happens to those waterways come January.
At the Environment Agency we’re encouraging farmers to look at slurry storage requirements before the rain arrives. Now is the time to start planning for next winter.
With pressure on fuel and fertiliser prices, having plenty of spare capacity is not only vital for compliance, but also saves a valuable resource for when it’s most needed.
From an environmental point of view, spreading slurry during the winter months creates a significant pollution risk from run-off, damages soils and wastes valuable nutrients.
Spreading because your store is full, rather than because there is a soil or crop need, is also non-compliant with environmental regulations.
How much slurry storage capacity do I need?
The Silage, Slurry and Fuel Oil Regulations set out that all farms must have at least 4 months slurry storage.
If you’re in a Nitrate Vulnerable Zone, that requirement is higher.  Check what applies to your livestock type.
Farming Rules for Water also say you should not apply more than the soil and crop actually need, and you should not create a pollution risk.
We recommend a minimum of 6 months slurry storage to ensure meeting the requirements of Farming Rules for Water.
What can I do to prepare my slurry storage for winter?

Guttering that leaks or drainage that isn’t functioning properly can lead to an increase in slurry volume as clean rainwater mixes with manure in yards. Fixing any leaky pipes and gutters and making sure drains are free and running properly can make a difference. You may find these changes alone mean that your existing storage meets your requirements.
Use the AHDB slurry wizard to check how much slurry storage you need – this will show you if have enough storage to be compliant and to see you through the winter.
It can also help with planning for the future to assess the levels of capacity you may need for farm expansion, or to give you a buffer for contingency.
If your calculations show that you may not have enough storage, look at contingencies and get a plan in place to increase your storage capacity.
3. Plan for all eventualities
Whether you think you have enough storage capacity or not, making contingency plans could help you through if something unexpected happens.
Options to consider:

Read more about the guidance around storing slurry and planning a new store including notifying the Environment Agency at least 14 days before you build new storage for slurry or make substantial changes to an existing store.

Farmers can access Defra funding to improve slurry storage and management through the Capital Grant offer, expected to open 30 July. The Grant will fund items like automatic slurry scrapers, self-supporting covers for slurry and anaerobic digestate stores  and floating covers for slurry and anaerobic digestate stores and lagoons. Read the full guidance for Capital Grants here - Applicant's guide: Capital Grants 2026 - GOV.UK

Being ready for winter can help your business all year round. Only applying organic fertiliser during the growing season means that crops and grass take up more of the nutrients, increasing yields. Keeping machinery off wet soils not only protects the soil, but saves unnecessary fuel, wear and tear and man hours.
See how a Cornish dairy farmer tackles slurry storage challenges and transforms his farm to meet regulations.
Get in touch
If you have questions about preparing for winter, we can help – contact our national customer contact centre and ask to be put in contact with your local agriculture team.
Environment Agency National Customer Contact Centre
Email: enquiries@environment-agency.gov.uk
Other resources:
Farming Advice Service: https://www.farmingadviceservice.org.uk/technical-article/environment-agency-winter-ready-cab-card
Catchment Sensitive Farming: Catchment Sensitive Farming: advice for farmers and land managers - GOV.UK (www.gov.uk)

title: New date for Capital Grants 2026 webinar

content.content: The 2026 Capital Grants is expected to open on 30 July.
To help you prepare, we're hosting a webinar on 30 July for you to find out more. This webinar has been rescheduled from the original date of 22 July.
During the session you'll hear from me, and colleagues from the Rural Payments Agency (RPA). We will also cover the support provided by Catchment Sensitive Farming (CSF) (look at section 4.2).
We will explain which grant items may need CSF advice before you apply, and RPA colleagues will take you through the application and claims process.
We'll finish with a Q&A session, giving you the chance to ask questions and get answers from the team.
The webinar will start at 11am and finish at 12:30pm.
Register to attend.
If you can’t make it, don’t worry. We will publish a link to the recording once the webinar finishes.
For more information ahead of the webinar, do read my previous posts on Capital Grants and the Capital Grants 2026 guidance on GOV.UK.
This new round will make £225 million available which is 50% more than in 2025.
I look forward to seeing you there.

title: Learn more about the Farmer Welfare Grant

content.content: Earlier this month, we wrote a post introducing the Farmer Welfare Grant.
A total of £1.5 million will be available over 3 years to support farmer mental health and wellbeing across England.
The funding is intended to help rural and agricultural charities and organisations deliver practical support that strengthens both personal and business resilience across the sector.

While the application portal will not open until 6 August, we are sharing additional information in advance to help organisations considering an application. This includes details of 2 upcoming webinars.
Guidance, including the technical eligibility criteria, will be available when the portal opens.
Who can apply
Funding is only available to organisations with experience of supporting farming communities, not for individual farm businesses.
Any charitable or third-sector not-for-profit organisation registered in England can apply for funding if it can demonstrate its ability to deliver a suitable project.

For-profit organisations may also be eligible to apply as part of a consortium led by an eligible organisation, provided they can demonstrate how both the project and their role contribute to meeting the funding criteria.

We want grant recipients to develop support that responds to the specific needs of farming communities. For this reason, we are not prescribing the types of activities or approaches applicants should propose.
That said, applications that support the following priorities are particularly encouraged:

Funding can be used to cover both one-off and ongoing costs. This may include overheads, venue hire, materials, equipment, service delivery costs, and staffing costs where these are directly related to the project.
The exact number of projects will be determined by the amount and nature of applications we receive.
We’ll consider both individual projects and joint projects involving multiple organisations.
Applications are invited for grants of between £1,000 and £200,000 per year, covering expenditure incurred between November 2026 and March 2029.
How to apply
To apply, you must do so through an application portal. We will blog again when the portal opens.
As part of the application, you'll need to:
Once the application window has closed, the applications will be reviewed and scored by a team from Defra. Funding decisions will be made after all applications have been assessed.
Dates to note
Thursday 6 August – Application portal opens. Full guidance available.
Thursday 13 August, 2pm–3pm – Join our first webinar to learn more about the grant, guidance and eligibility criteria. A recording will be shared in this post after the session.
Monday 17 August, 10am–11am – Join our second webinar for a walkthrough of the application portal and application process. A recording will be shared in this post after the session
Wednesday 9 September, 11:59 am– Application portal closes.

For the latest updates on the Farmer Welfare Grant, subscribe to the Farming Blog.
By subscribing, you'll receive an email notification whenever we publish a new blog post.
